title.en: Hello from Earth · opening screen

text.en: Oops! Soft landing... mostly. Hi! I'm VIMO. I'm an astronaut, and I look after some very special friends. They live far, far away.

title.en: Hello from Earth

text.en: Wait, VIMO, who lives up there?
Machines! Cameras, landers, rovers, even a helicopter. NASA sent them to the Moon and Mars to explore. When their work was done, they stayed there.

title.en: Hello from Earth · the purpose

text.en: Some people call them space junk. I don't. Each one has a story: where it went, what it did, and what it taught us. Tonight, you and I will visit them. Ready?

title.en: Why is space hard?

text.en: See that thin blue line? That's our air. Above it is space: no air to breathe, no sound, and it's freezing in the shade and boiling in the sunlight.

title.en: Why is space hard?

text.en: Why can't we just fly up there?
Earth pulls everything down. That's gravity. To escape it, a rocket must go about 40,000 kilometres per hour. That's 30 times faster than a jet plane!

title.en: Why is space hard? · how far is the Moon?

text.en: If Earth were a basketball, the Moon would be a tennis ball about seven metres away. In real life that's about 384,000 kilometres. In a car, it would take you more than 5 months, with no stops!

title.en: Lift-off to the Moon

text.en: Hold on tight! Three... two... one... lift-off! Our first stop is 1964, when NASA was still learning how to even reach the Moon.

title.en: The big map

text.en: Every glowing pin is a machine NASA sent out there. Watch them appear, year by year!

changed.from: (storyboard Act 2) Every glowing pin is a machine NASA sent out there. Fifty-seven friends, and every one of them is still out there!
changed.why: Removed "Fifty-seven friends… every one still out there" (count comes from the Hardware Atlas, not a checked NASA page); added the year-by-year cue for the counter.

title.en: Place tour: the Moon

text.en: Up here on the Moon: cameras that crashed on purpose, landers, and three cars!

changed.from: (storyboard Act 2) The Moon is about three days away by rocket. Up here: cameras that crashed on purpose, landers, three cars... even a golf ball!
changed.why: Removed "about three days by rocket" (unverified) and the golf ball (Apollo 14 side trip, unverified). Three cars: three rovers were used (NSSDCA LRV page).

title.en: Place tour: Mars

text.en: Mars is much farther. Rovers, landers, parachutes and even a little helicopter live here.

changed.from: (storyboard Act 2) Mars is much farther: about seven months by rocket! Rovers, landers, parachutes and even a little helicopter live here.
changed.why: Removed "about seven months by rocket" (launch date not on a checked page yet).

title.en: Place tour: still traveling

text.en: And some never landed at all. They're still flying away from the Sun. Even my jetpack can't catch them!

title.en: Lift-off to the Moon · on the way

text.en: Fun fact: in space there's no up or down, so I can read upside down. Look, the year counter! We're going back in time to 1964. That's before your grandparents were teenagers, maybe!

title.en: Big question

text.en: Big question: how did we learn to land on the Moon, and what still works there today?

title.en: The camera that fell (Ranger 7, 1964) · Where

text.en: Meet Ranger 7! In 1964, nobody had ever seen the Moon up close. So NASA sent a camera... and let it crash.
Crash? On purpose?!

title.en: The camera that fell (Ranger 7, 1964) · What and how

text.en: Click! Click! Click! I took pictures all the way down. I didn't need to land. I just needed to look!
In its last 17 minutes, Ranger 7 sent more than 4,000 photos. They were the closest pictures of the Moon anyone had ever seen.

archie.title: Live from the Moon – Impact!
archie.why: Ranger 9's real pictures, falling into Alphonsus crater.

text.en: See? The closer you get, the more you can see.

title.en: The camera that fell (Ranger 7, 1964) · Now + goodbye

text.en: Scientists even gave the place a new name: the Sea that has Become Known. Ranger 7 is still there, in pieces, right where it learned the Moon's first secrets. Thank you, Ranger 7!

title.en: The first soft step (Surveyor 1, 1966) · The big question

text.en: Some scientists worried the Moon was covered in deep dust. Like soft flour. Would a spacecraft sink? Would an astronaut sink? Someone had to test it.

title.en: The first soft step (Surveyor 1, 1966) · Landing

text.en: Touchdown! And look: my feet are on top of the dust, not under it. The ground is strong!
Surveyor 1 was America's first soft landing on the Moon. It sent more than 11,000 photos. Now NASA knew: people could land here too.
So that's how rockets slow you down.

title.en: The first soft step (Surveyor 1, 1966) · How + goodbye

text.en: Thank you, Surveyor 1. You took the Moon's first safe step, so astronauts could take the next one.

title.en: The robot who got a visit (Surveyor 3 + Apollo 12) · Lonely robot

text.en: This is Surveyor 3. It landed in 1967, dug the Moon's soil with a little scoop, and sent photos home. Then it went quiet. Alone. For two and a half years.
...beep... is anyone... coming?

title.en: The robot who got a visit (Surveyor 3 + Apollo 12) · The visit

text.en: Then, in November 1969, Apollo 12 landed close by. Two astronauts walked over to say hello!
Visitors! I knew someone would come back.

archie.title: Astronauts Pay a Visit to Surveyor 3
archie.why: The real photo of an astronaut beside the robot.

title.en: The robot who got a visit (Surveyor 3 + Apollo 12) · Bringing pieces home

text.en: Why did they take its camera?
To see what two and a half years on the Moon does to a machine. Its parts came home for scientists to study. Surveyor 3 helped us twice!

changed.from: To see what two and a half years on the Moon does to metal, glass and paint. Its parts came home for scientists to study. Surveyor 3 helped us twice!
changed.why: docs/05 video 03 (checked): parts came home so engineers could see what the Moon does to a machine. "Metal, glass and paint" is not on the page.

title.en: The robot who got a visit (Surveyor 3 + Apollo 12) · Intrepid, the lander that parked next door

text.en: I landed so precisely that the astronauts could walk to an old robot parked nearby.
Apollo 12 also left a science station. When its top part was crashed into the Moon later, the Moon 'rang' like a bell for nearly an hour!

changed.from: Apollo 12 also left the first full science station. When its top part was crashed into the Moon later, the Moon 'rang' like a bell for about an hour!
changed.why: NASA page says "nearly an hour" (docs/05 video 04); "first full science station" is not on the checked page.

archie.title: LRO Looks at Apollo 12, Surveyor 3 Landing Sites
archie.why: Both machines, seen from orbit today.

text.en: So that's how we listen to the inside of the Moon.

title.en: The Eagle's bottom half (Apollo 11, 1969) · Where

text.en: This is it. July 1969. The first time people walked on another world. And this is their ship, the Eagle.

title.en: The Eagle's bottom half (Apollo 11, 1969) · The trick

text.en: Hey, half of it stayed behind!
That's the plan! The bottom half was the launch pad. The astronauts flew home in the top half. The bottom half is still standing there today.

title.en: The Eagle's bottom half (Apollo 11, 1969) · The plaque

text.en: My plaque says: 'We came in peace for all mankind.' I've been holding that message for more than 55 years.
Footprints, tools and the Eagle's bottom half are all still there. There's no wind on the Moon, so footprints can last a very long time.

title.en: The mirror that still answers (1969 → today) · The secret

text.en: Most of the machines we visit tonight are finished. But this little box is still working. Right now. Watch!

title.en: The mirror that still answers (1969 → today) · The laser

text.en: Ping! Ping! Every beam you send, I send back. Same way, every time!
Scientists measure how long the light takes. That's how we know the Moon is moving away from Earth, about 3.8 centimetres every year. That's how fast your fingernails grow!

archie.title: The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving
archie.why: How the mirrors are still used.

text.en: So that's how light measures the distance to the Moon.

title.en: A car on the Moon (Apollo 15 rover, 1971) · Unfolding

text.en: Boing... boing... And in 1971, astronauts brought a car! It came folded up, like a paper toy.

changed.from: Boing... boing... On the Moon you weigh about one sixth of your weight on Earth. And in 1971, astronauts brought a car! It came folded up, like a paper toy.
changed.why: Removed "you weigh about one sixth" (no checked NASA page yet).

title.en: A car on the Moon (Apollo 15 rover, 1971) · The drive

text.en: Battery power, wire-mesh wheels and no road at all. I drove the astronauts about 28 kilometres. Not bad for a car that fits in a suitcase... a big suitcase.
Why mesh wheels and not rubber tyres?
No air means no air-filled tyres. So its wheels were woven from thin steel wire, like a basket!

changed.from: Rubber can crack in the Moon's huge cold and heat, and air tyres can pop. Metal mesh wheels can't go flat.
changed.why: Script asked to confirm the tyre reason; docs/05 video 07 (checked) gives this wording.

title.en: A car on the Moon (Apollo 15 rover, 1971) · Parking the rover

text.en: The rover is still parked there, waiting. But Apollo isn't finished yet. More astronauts are coming!

title.en: The last footsteps (Apollo 17, 1972) · Duct tape

text.en: When my fender broke, the astronauts fixed it with duct tape and maps. Good as new!
Even on the Moon, sometimes the best tool is tape!

archie.title: Apollo 17 video library
archie.why: Real film: the fender taped, then the lift-off.

text.en: Astronauts fix things with what they have!

title.en: The last footsteps (Apollo 17, 1972) · The last goodbye

text.en: In December 1972, the last astronauts left the Moon. Nobody has walked here since. Not yet.
Not yet? Will people go back?
NASA is planning to! But first, let's see who is still watching the Moon.

changed.from: NASA is planning to! But first, let's see the robots that went back in the meantime.
changed.why: Side trips now come after the ending, so the next stop is LRO, not "the robots that went back".

title.en: The Moon's photographer (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, 2009 → today) · Still watching

text.en: I'm the Moon's photographer. From orbit I can still see the Apollo landers, rover tracks and even footpaths.
So it's true. They're all still there, right where they finished their work. LRO is still working today.

title.en: The answer so far

text.en: The answer so far: robots scouted first, people followed, and the mirrors and LRO still send us science.

title.en: The Moon's photographer (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, 2009 → today) · Goodbye to the Moon

text.en: So many friends on the Moon! Now hold on. Our next trip is much, much longer. Next stop: Mars!

changed.from: So many friends on the Moon! Now hold on. Our next trip is much, much longer. Let's jump back to 1971... next stop: Mars!
changed.why: Removed "jump back to 1971" (that is Mariner 9, now a side trip after the ending).

title.en: Big question

text.en: Big question: could Mars once have been a home for tiny life?

title.en: The long flight to Mars · How far?

text.en: The Moon took three days. Mars takes about seven months! And we can't fly straight at it. Mars keeps moving, so we aim for where it will be.
Like throwing a ball to a friend who's running?
Exactly like that!

title.en: The long flight to Mars · The message delay

text.en: A radio message to Mars takes up to 22 minutes! So nobody can drive a Mars robot with a joystick. The robots have to be smart and careful on their own.

changed.from: A radio message to Mars takes up to 20 minutes! So nobody can drive a Mars robot with a joystick. The robots have to be smart and careful on their own.
changed.why: Checked NASA page (Build Spec §8, docs/05): 3 to 22 minutes, not "up to 20".

title.en: The long flight to Mars · Hello, Mars

text.en: Mars is red because its dust has rust in it, like an old iron gate. It's colder than any freezer, and its air is so thin you couldn't breathe even for a second.

title.en: The first Mars photo (Viking 1, 1976) · Landing day

text.en: July 20th, 1976: exactly seven years after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, Viking 1 landed safely on Mars.

changed.from: July 20th, 1976: exactly seven years after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, Viking 1 landed safely on Mars. NASA's first!
changed.why: Removed "NASA's first!" (not stated on the checked Viking page). "Seven years" is our calculation from two checked dates.

title.en: The first Mars photo (Viking 1, 1976) · The first picture

text.en: The first thing I photographed on Mars? My own foot. I wanted to check I'd landed on something solid!
Viking 1 sent the first pictures ever taken on the surface of Mars. It also tested the soil, looking for tiny signs of life.
Did it find aliens?
No aliens! Scientists still talk about what its soil tests meant. That's okay. In science, 'we're not sure yet' is an honest answer.

archie.title: First Photograph Taken on Mars Surface
archie.why: The original first picture, full size.

title.en: The first Mars photo (Viking 1, 1976) · Now + goodbye

text.en: Viking 1 kept working for more than six years. It went quiet in 1982 and is still sitting on that plain. Thank you, Viking!

title.en: The first Mars rover (Mars Pathfinder + Sojourner, 1997) · Bounce, bounce, bounce

text.en: After Viking, Mars waited 21 years. Then, on the 4th of July 1997, a new lander arrived. Boing! Boing! Boing! It landed in a ball of airbags!

title.en: The first Mars rover (Mars Pathfinder + Sojourner, 1997) · The tiny rover

text.en: I'm the first rover on Mars, as small as a microwave oven. I never went more than a few metres from my lander, but I was the first!
Sojourner was the first rover on another planet. Tiny, but it proved a rover can drive on another planet.

changed.from: Sojourner was the first wheeled robot on another planet. Every Mars rover after it, even the giant ones, came from this little explorer.
changed.why: "Every Mars rover after it came from this little explorer" is not on the checked page; docs/05 video 11 wording used.

title.en: 90 days that became 14 years (Opportunity, 2004–2018) · The bouncy landing

text.en: Opportunity landed in a giant ball of airbags, bounced, and rolled straight into a little crater. A hole in one!

title.en: 90 days that became 14 years (Opportunity, 2004–2018) · The promise

text.en: They told me I'd work for 90 days. I just... kept going. I drove more than a marathon: 45 kilometres!
Opportunity was planned for 90 days and explored for more than 14 years!

title.en: 90 days that became 14 years (Opportunity, 2004–2018) · The water clue

text.en: What's so special about this rock?
It has hematite, a mineral that forms in water. So long ago, Mars had water!
Hematite forms in water. Mars was once wet here!

title.en: 90 days that became 14 years (Opportunity, 2004–2018) · The dust storm the sad moment

text.en: In 2018, a huge dust storm covered the whole planet. The Sun was hidden, and Opportunity's solar panels couldn't make power.

changed.from: In 2018, a huge dust storm covered the whole planet. The Sun was hidden, and Opportunity's solar panels couldn't make power. Its last message just said: power very low, sky very dark.
changed.why: Removed the quoted "last message" (not on NASA's page; docs/05 and doc 07 forbid invented quotes).

text.en: NASA called to it more than 1,000 times. It never answered. But it had done its job, and much, much more.

title.en: 90 days that became 14 years (Opportunity, 2004–2018) · Goodbye

text.en: Goodbye, Oppy. Built for 90 days, you gave us almost 15 years. You are not forgotten.

title.en: A rover as big as a car (Curiosity, 2012 → today) · The sky crane

text.en: Curiosity is as big as a car, too heavy for airbags. So NASA lowered it on ropes from a flying rocket crane. And look: every landing leaves parts behind, like breadcrumbs.
We protected the rovers through a fiery fall, then dropped away. Now we lie in the dust like a trail of breadcrumbs.

title.en: A rover as big as a car (Curiosity, 2012 → today) · Reading Mars like a book

text.en: I'm climbing a mountain in an old lake bed, reading Mars's history layer by layer, like pages in a book.
Curiosity showed that Gale crater once held a lake where tiny living things, microbes, could have lived. And it's still working today!

title.en: Listening to Mars (InSight, 2018–2022) · The heartbeat

text.en: I put my ear to the ground and heard Mars rumble more than a thousand times.
InSight recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and learned about Mars' core. Like a doctor listening to a heartbeat!

title.en: Listening to Mars (InSight, 2018–2022) · Dusty goodbye

text.en: Bit by bit, dust covered its solar panels. In December 2022, InSight went quiet. Thank you for listening, InSight.

title.en: The parachute with a secret (Perseverance, 2021) · Seven minutes

text.en: Landing on Mars takes about seven minutes, and the robot must do it all by itself. NASA engineers call it 'seven minutes of terror'!

title.en: The parachute with a secret (Perseverance, 2021) · The leftovers

text.en: Sure, I'm lying in the sand now. But I protected Perseverance on the way down. You're welcome!

changed.from: Sure, I'm lying in the sand now. But I protected Perseverance from heat hotter than lava. You're welcome!
changed.why: Removed "heat hotter than lava" (not on the checked pages).

text.en: These parts were used only once, for a few minutes. But without them, Perseverance couldn't have landed.

changed.from: These parts were used only once, for seven minutes. But without them, Perseverance couldn't have landed.
changed.why: "Seven minutes" is unverified; docs/05 video 15 says "a few minutes".

archie.title: Perseverance landing video
archie.why: The real parachute opening and sky crane.

title.en: The parachute with a secret (Perseverance, 2021) · The secret code

text.en: Psst... the parachute has a secret message hidden in its pattern. Engineers wrote it in computer code. Can you crack it?
Engineers have fun too!

title.en: Wings over Mars (Ingenuity, 2021–2024) · The tiny helicopter

text.en: This little helicopter is Ingenuity. It weighs about the same as two big bottles of water. Its job: try to fly on another planet. Nobody had ever done that.
But you said Mars has almost no air!
Right! So its blades spin super fast, about 2,400 times a minute. That's much faster than a helicopter on Earth.

title.en: Wings over Mars (Ingenuity, 2021–2024) · First flight

text.en: I was supposed to fly 5 times. I flew 72 times!

changed.from: I was supposed to fly 5 times. I flew 72 times! I even scouted the path for my big friend, Perseverance.
changed.why: Removed "scouted the path for Perseverance" (not on the checked pages).

text.en: The first powered flight on another planet! It was planned for five test flights. It flew 72!

title.en: Wings over Mars (Ingenuity, 2021–2024) · Now + goodbye

text.en: In January 2024, on its 72nd flight, a blade broke, so it can't fly anymore. But every day it still wakes up, checks itself and saves data for future explorers who come to visit. A little hero, waiting on a sandy hill.

changed.from: In January 2024, on its 72nd flight, a blade broke, so it can't fly anymore. But every day it still wakes up, checks itself and takes a photo, saving the data for future explorers who come to visit. A little hero, waiting on a sandy hill.
changed.why: JPL page says it wakes daily to test systems and record data; "takes a photo" is not stated.

text.en: And Perseverance is still out there, exploring. Keep going, Percy!

title.en: Pieces of Mars, waiting for a ride (Perseverance + Three Forks, 2021 → today) · The sample collector

text.en: I'm collecting pieces of Mars in little tubes, so that one day scientists on Earth can study them.
Perseverance is searching this old river delta for signs of past life. And it's still working today!

title.en: Pieces of Mars, waiting for a ride (Perseverance + Three Forks, 2021 → today) · The tubes left on purpose

text.en: We are ten little tubes of Mars rock, left on the ground on purpose, waiting for a ride to Earth.
This is the first sample depot on another planet. These tubes aren't abandoned. They're waiting. Just like all our friends.

title.en: The answer so far

text.en: The answer so far: Mars once had water and places where life could have lived. The samples may tell us more.

title.en: Pieces of Mars, waiting for a ride (Perseverance + Three Forks, 2021 → today) · Goodbye to Mars

text.en: Mars, thank you! But some machines went even farther. Much, much farther. Ready?

title.en: Big question

text.en: Big question: how far can a machine we built travel?

title.en: Still traveling (Pioneer 10 and Voyager 1) · Leaving everything behind

text.en: Some machines never landed anywhere. They're still flying away from the Sun! Even my jetpack can't catch them.

title.en: Still traveling (Pioneer 10 and Voyager 1) · Pioneer 10

text.en: 1972... I was the first to fly past Jupiter... I sent my last message in 2003. I'm still flying, quietly.
Pioneer 10 carries a metal plaque with a drawing that shows where it came from: Earth.

title.en: Still traveling (Pioneer 10 and Voyager 1) · Voyager 2, the only visitor

text.en: I'm the only visitor Uranus and Neptune have ever had.

changed.from: I'm the only visitor Uranus and Neptune have ever had, and I carry a golden record of Earth's music.
changed.why: Golden record on Voyager 2 is not on the checked Voyager 2 page.

text.en: Voyager 2 went into interstellar space in 2018. It's still sending data home today.

changed.from: Voyager 2 went into interstellar space in 2018, about 21 billion kilometres away. It's still working, on very low power.
changed.why: "About 21 billion km" and "very low power" are not on the checked page; docs/05 video 19 wording used.

slides.text: Only visitor to Uranus and Neptune

title.en: Still traveling (Pioneer 10 and Voyager 1) · Voyager 1

text.en: Launched in 1977. I'm the farthest thing people have ever made. I carry a golden record with sounds and music from Earth. And yes... I still call home.
On 18 November 2026, Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: its signal will take a whole day to reach us! It's in interstellar space, between the stars.

archie.title: Voyager 1's Pale Blue Dot
archie.why: Earth as 'a point of light about a pixel in size'.

title.en: Pluto's heart (New Horizons, 2006 → today) · A heart in the dark

text.en: I showed the world Pluto's heart-shaped glacier.

changed.from: I showed the world Pluto's heart-shaped glacier, and I carry the man who discovered Pluto.
changed.why: Final Review cut the Tombaugh ashes line (not on the NASA pages used).

text.en: After Pluto, New Horizons flew past Arrokoth in 2019, the farthest world ever explored up close. It's still working!

title.en: The answer so far

text.en: The answer so far: out of the Sun's bubble, one light-day away, and still calling home.

title.en: VIMO's logbook · The big idea

text.en: Look at all our friends! Some still work. Some went quiet. Some were used once, on purpose. But none of them are just junk. Each one taught us something.

title.en: VIMO's logbook · The sorting game

text.en: See? Old doesn't mean abandoned. They're resting where they finished their work.

title.en: Home · Flying home

text.en: Perfect landing! See, I'm learning too.

title.en: Home · Looking up

text.en: Next time you look at the Moon, remember: there's a lander's bottom half up there, a car, footprints... and a little mirror that still answers when we call.

title.en: Home · The next chapter

text.en: And the story isn't over. In April 2026, four astronauts flew around the Moon, farther from Earth than any humans ever. NASA plans to land people near the Moon's south pole in 2028.

archie.title: Artemis II crew back on Earth
archie.why: The record-setting Artemis II astronauts, home after flying around the Moon.

title.en: Home · The last line

text.en: These machines were brave enough to go first. Maybe one day you'll build the next one. And when it finishes its work, someone like me will come and say thank you.
